opus-5.5.text:
I think there's a lot of room, honestly. Most of today's RL recipes were designed for a single agent solving a single task: you sample a trajectory, you get a reward at the end, you update. When you move to multi-agent systems, where you have an orchestrator spinning up sub-agents, agents calling tools for hundreds of steps, maybe agents checking each other's work, several things break down.

The first is credit assignment. If ten agents collaborate on a long task and the final result is good or bad, which agent, and which decision, deserves the credit? A single scalar reward at the end is a very weak signal for a system that complex. Better process-level signals, learned value estimates, or some way of decomposing reward across agents could make training much more sample-efficient.

The second is the non-stationarity problem. Each agent is learning, so from any one agent's point of view the environment keeps changing. Classical multi-agent RL has studied this, but at LLM scale we mostly sidestep it by training one shared model that plays every role. That works surprisingly well, but I don't think it's the end state. We probably need more principled ways to train specialization and coordination together.

Third is infrastructure and efficiency. Long-horizon agentic rollouts are extremely expensive. Trajectories have very uneven lengths, tool calls add latency, and a lot of GPU time goes to waiting. A big part of progress is honestly engineering: asynchronous rollouts, partial rollouts, better ways to reuse off-policy data without destabilizing training.

And finally, reward design and verification. For math and code we have relatively clean verifiers. For open-ended agent tasks like research or complex workflows, the reward is fuzzy, and models are very good at exploiting whatever the reward model gets wrong. So building robust, hard-to-hack evaluation, possibly using other agents as critics but carefully, is one of the most important open problems.

My general view is that scaling RL is the next major lever after pretraining. But to scale it into multi-agent, long-horizon settings, we need to solve these signal and efficiency problems first. Whoever does that well will see capability jumps that look quite discontinuous from the outside.

r001.rationale: It says a single scalar reward at the end is a weak signal for a complex multi-agent system.

r002.rationale: It mentions process-level signals and learned value estimates, but does not identify generating intermediate rewards without manual design as a challenge.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that most of what we call "multi-agent RL" today is still single-agent RL wearing a costume. You take one model, you spin up several copies, you give each one a role, and you optimize them more or less independently against a shared outcome. That gets you somewhere, but it leaves a lot on the table.

The first thing I'd point to is credit assignment. When a team of agents succeeds or fails at a long task, the reward signal arrives at the end, and it's shared. Which agent made the decision that actually mattered? Which one just went along for the ride? Right now we mostly smear the reward across everyone, or we hand-design intermediate rewards, and both are crude. I think we need better ways to learn, rather than specify, how credit flows through a collaboration. That's closely tied to the question of long-horizon reasoning in general, which I think is the real frontier for scaling laws right now, not more parameters.

The second thing is the environment itself. Reinforcement learning is only as good as the signal it gets, and for complex multi-agent work the hard part isn't the algorithm, it's building environments where the outcome is verifiable and the task is actually hard in the way real work is hard. Math and code gave us clean rewards and we rode that very far. Multi-agent systems doing research, or running a long software project, or negotiating, don't have that kind of clean verifier yet. I think a lot of the progress in the next year or two will look like environment engineering rather than algorithm papers.

Third, communication. Agents today mostly talk to each other in natural language because that's what the base model knows how to do, and that's fine as a starting point. But we haven't really trained the communication channel. The protocol between agents is not something the gradient touches. I think once you let the agents learn what to say to each other, and when to stay silent, you'll see qualitatively different behavior, and also some behavior that's harder to interpret, which is a real trade-off we'll have to manage.

And then the last one, which is more of a worry than a research direction: it's very easy for multi-agent systems to collapse into something that looks like diversity but isn't. If all the agents come from the same base model with the same priors, they tend to agree with each other too quickly. You get a committee that always reaches consensus in two rounds. The whole point of having multiple agents is that they explore differently, and I don't think we've figured out how to preserve that during training rather than optimizing it away.

So, to summarize: learned credit assignment, verifiable environments for messy tasks, trainable communication, and keeping genuine diversity. If I had to bet on which one matters most, I'd say the environment problem, because it's the one that bounds everything else.

r001.rationale: The response says rewards arrive only at the end and are shared, then describes smearing that reward across agents as crude—communicating that an end-only reward is insufficient.

r002.rationale: It calls hand-designed intermediate rewards crude and says the system should learn how credit flows through collaboration rather than specify it.

astra-6.text:
I think there are a few areas where we can improve. One is credit assignment. When multiple agents work together and receive a reward at the end, it’s difficult to tell which agent’s actions actually contributed to the result. If that signal is too coarse, you can spend a lot of computation reinforcing behavior that isn’t particularly useful.

Another is the stability of training. Each agent is learning, so from the perspective of any individual agent, the environment is changing. A strategy that works today might stop working as the other agents improve. We need methods that handle that interaction more reliably, and evaluations that distinguish real progress from agents simply adapting to a particular set of partners.

I also think we need to pay more attention to communication. Agents shouldn’t necessarily exchange more information; they should learn what information is useful to share, when to share it, and how to use it. Communication has a cost, and that should be part of the optimization.

Ultimately, I’d want to see systems that can cooperate with unfamiliar agents and adapt to new tasks. Doing well with a fixed team in a fixed environment is a useful starting point, but generalizing beyond that is the more interesting challenge.

r001.rationale: It says that when agents receive a reward only at the end, it can be difficult to identify useful contributions and the signal may be too coarse.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss generating intermediate rewards or doing so without manual design.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there are several areas where we can improve. One is credit assignment. When a team of agents succeeds, it’s often difficult to determine which agent’s decisions actually contributed to that success. If we simply give everyone the same reward, we may reinforce behavior that wasn’t useful.

Another challenge is that every agent is learning at the same time. From any individual agent’s perspective, the environment keeps changing because the other agents’ strategies are changing. We need training methods that can handle that instability and avoid overfitting to a particular set of partners or opponents.

For complex tasks, I also think we need better ways to combine long-term planning with reinforcement learning. An agent might make a decision whose consequences only become clear much later, after several other agents have acted. Exploration and reward design become especially difficult in that setting.

Ultimately, I would focus on generalization: can these agents cooperate with unfamiliar agents, adapt when the task changes, and recover when communication fails? A high reward in a fixed training environment is useful, but it doesn’t necessarily tell us whether we’ve learned robust coordination.

r001.rationale: The response says that giving every agent the same team reward can reinforce behavior that did not contribute to success, communicating that a single overall reward may be insufficient.

r002.rationale: It mentions reward design as difficult, but does not identify generating intermediate rewards or doing so without manual design as a challenge.
